reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I capital, EUR: ordinary equity 150m, subordinated debt with original maturity over 5 years 50m, and perpetual cumulative preferred stock 20m. No noncumulative preferred is held.

options.label: EUR 50m
options.why: Put the cumulative preferred into Tier 1 (giving Tier 1 = 170m) and left only the subordinated debt in Tier 2.

options.label: EUR 20m
options.why: Counted only the preferred and dropped the subordinated debt, which is also Tier 2.

working.label: Limit check
working.display: Tier 2 of 70 is below half of total capital (110 of 220), so all of it counts

takeaway: Basel I: only equity and noncumulative perpetual preferred are Tier 1. Cumulative preferred sits in Tier 2 with qualifying subordinated debt.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II capital adequacy. A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2 billion.
ask: The capital adequacy ratio is closest to:

options.why: Left the ratio as the decimal 0.15 and then wrote a percent sign.
Read RWA as USD 200m (dropped a zero from 2 billion), so 300 / 200.
Inverted the ratio: RWA / capital = 2,000 / 300.

takeaway: CAR uses total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) over RWA. Keep millions and billions on the same scale before dividing.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel 2.5 standardized charges for a correlation book. Positions: a USD 60m AA securitization tranche (1.6%), a USD 25m BBB re-securitization tranche (18% on the re-securitization schedule) and an USD 8m unrated securitization tranche (100%).
ask: Which position carries the largest capital charge?

options.label: The USD 60m AA tranche
options.why: Followed the largest notional. At 1.6% it charges only USD 0.96m.

options.label: The USD 25m BBB re-securitization
options.why: Looked at the middle size and rating: 25 × 18% = USD 4.50m, still short of the unrated tranche.

takeaway: Unrated and below-BB positions are charged dollar for dollar, so the smallest position can dominate the capital charge.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel III bank, USD m: common stock 730, unrealized gain on long-term marketable equity securities 33, five-year subordinated debt 28, goodwill 92. Tier 1 is common stock plus the unrealized gain, less goodwill.
ask: Tier 1 capital compared with the USD 730m of common stock is:

options.label: Above USD 730m
options.why: Added the gain and forgot that goodwill is deducted, or even added it: 730 + 33 = 763.

options.label: Equal to USD 730m
options.why: Treated the gain and the goodwill as offsetting. They are 33 up against 92 down.

takeaway: Goodwill is deducted from Tier 1, and here it outweighs the unrealized gain, so Tier 1 sits below common stock.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel III balance sheet, EUR m: common equity 2,010; non-callable preferred equity 500; subordinated debt 1,500; retained earnings 3,210; goodwill 850. RWA are EUR 49,700m.
ask: The Core Tier 1 (CET1) capital in the numerator is:

options.label: EUR 4,870m
options.why: Counted the preferred equity, which is Additional Tier 1, not CET1.

options.label: EUR 5,220m
options.why: Forgot to deduct goodwill: 2,010 + 3,210.

options.label: EUR 6,370m
options.why: Counted the preferred equity and the subordinated debt (Tier 2) as well.

takeaway: CET1 is common equity plus retained earnings, less goodwill and intangibles. Preferred shares and subordinated debt belong to other tiers.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Prime Bank has RWA of USD 200m. Under fully phased-in Basel III it must meet the CET1 minimum plus the capital conservation buffer (ignore any G-SIB or countercyclical buffer).
ask: The CET1 ratio it must hold is:

options.why: Used the CET1 minimum alone and left the conservation buffer out.
Built on the 6% Tier 1 minimum instead of the 4.5% CET1 minimum: 6.0% + 2.5%.
Built on the 8% total capital minimum: 8.0% + 2.5%.

takeaway: The conservation buffer is stacked on the CET1 minimum and must itself be CET1, so the requirement is 7.0%, not a total-capital figure.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel III CET1 buffer zone: with a 2.5% conservation buffer it runs from 4.5% to 7.0%, split into four equal quartiles. Minimum earnings retained, lowest to highest quartile: 100%, 80%, 60%, 40% (0% above the zone). A bank has CET1 of 6.0%. A 2.5% countercyclical buffer is then switched on, widening the zone to 4.5%–9.5%.
ask: Its maximum dividend, as a percent of earnings, compared with before the switch-on:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed a larger buffer means more room. The same 6.0% now sits in a lower quartile of a wider zone.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Kept the old quartile width of 0.625%. With the wider zone each quartile is 1.25%.

working.label: Before: zone 4.5%–7.0%
working.display: Quartiles of 0.625%; 6.0% is in the 3rd, so retain 60% and pay up to 40%

working.label: After: zone 4.5%–9.5%
working.display: Quartiles of 1.25%; 6.0% is in the 2nd, so retain 80% and pay up to 20%

takeaway: A bigger buffer stretches the zone, so the same CET1 ratio falls into a lower quartile and the payout allowed shrinks.

reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
setup: Basel operational loss event. Gross loss USD 5,000,000. Forgone revenue (opportunity cost) USD 3,000,000. An estimated recovery of USD 1,500,000, 50% likely, none received yet. Insurance premiums of USD 12,500 paid while the event ran.
ask: The operational loss recorded for the event compared with the USD 5.0m gross loss is:

options.label: Above the gross loss
options.why: Added the forgone revenue. Opportunity cost is not a P&L charge, expense or provision, so it is not in the loss.

options.label: Below the gross loss
options.why: Netted the recovery, even probability-weighted (5.00 − 0.75 = 4.25). A recovery only reduces the loss once it is received.

takeaway: Gross loss counts direct charges only: no opportunity cost, no premiums, and no recovery until the cash is in.

setup: Fault tree for a rogue trader. Five independent conditions must ALL occur: 20%, 1%, 30%, 30% and 50%. A rogue event costs USD 100m. The firm has 1,000 traders, each with the same probabilities.
ask: Expected annual loss for the firm is closest to:

options.label: USD 9,000
options.why: Stopped at one trader and forgot to scale to 1,000 traders.

options.label: USD 50,000,000
options.why: Used only the last condition: 50% × USD 100m. All five conditions must hold together, so the probabilities multiply.

options.label: USD 900,000,000
options.why: Read the joint probability 0.009% as 0.9%, a factor of 100 too large.

takeaway: In an AND gate the probabilities multiply, so five conditions shrink the odds fast; then scale by the number of traders.

setup: Fault tree for a phishing-driven data leak, all events independent. The phishing email arrives: 99%. The firewall works as intended: 95%. The leak path needs the email to arrive AND to get past the firewall, before the later nodes (employee, detective controls, leak) are applied.
ask: After those first two nodes the running probability is closest to:

options.why: Used the firewall's success probability (0.95) instead of its failure probability (0.05): 0.99 × 0.95.
Ignored the firewall node altogether.

takeaway: A control node enters a fault tree through its failure probability, because the loss path needs the control to fail.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II standardized approach, Year 1 gross income (USD m): corporate finance 11.9 at a 17.99% multiplier, retail banking −26.2 at a 12.11% multiplier. The year's figure is the multiplier-weighted sum across the two lines.

options.label: Positive
options.why: Dropped the sign on the retail loss and added it: 2.14 + 3.17 = +5.31.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Applied a floor at zero to the sum. The arithmetic itself gives a nonzero number: the loss line outweighs the profit line.

takeaway: A negative business-line income offsets the other lines inside the year, and here it tips the year's total below zero.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II basic indicator approach (alpha 15%). Total annual gross income across all business lines, USD m: Year 1 65, Year 2 71, Year 3 74, all positive.
ask: Operational risk capital is closest to (USD m):

options.why: Averaged and then divided by 3 a second time.
Applied 15% to the three-year sum without averaging.
Used alpha as 1.5 instead of 15%, a factor of 10 too large.

takeaway: The basic indicator approach is 15% of average positive gross income. Business-line multipliers belong to the standardized approach.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II standardized approach. A bank's multiplier-weighted capital by year (USD m): Year 1 +11.17, Year 2 −0.88, Year 3 +12.48. A year whose total is negative is ignored in the average, not entered as zero.
ask: Required capital compared with the Year 1 figure of 11.17 is:

options.label: Below 11.17
options.why: Kept the negative year in the average: (11.17 − 0.88 + 12.48)/3 = 7.59. Entering zero instead would still give 7.88.

options.label: Equal to 11.17
options.why: Used the first year's figure alone.

takeaway: Dropping the negative year raises the average to 11.83, whereas a three-year average with the negative year in it gives only 7.59.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: EU securitization risk retention. A loan pool is tranched into a USD 320m senior, a USD 50m mezzanine and a USD 30m equity tranche. The originator must retain at least 5% of each tranche.
ask: The minimum total retained is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.5m
options.why: Retained 5% of the equity tranche only.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.0m
options.why: Applied 5% to the mezzanine and equity tranches only, leaving out the large senior tranche.

options.label: ≈ USD 200m
options.why: Read 5% as 50% of the USD 400m pool.

takeaway: Retention of 5% of each tranche equals 5% of the whole pool, and the senior tranche is where most of it sits.

reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
setup: Basel III standardized approach, business indicator, annual averages in EUR m: interest income 1,100; interest expense 380; interest-earning assets 40,000; dividend income 20. In the interest, leases and dividend component, absolute net interest income is capped at 2.25% of interest-earning assets, then dividend income is added.
ask: The interest, leases and dividend component is:

options.label: EUR 920m
options.why: Took the cap (2.25% × 40,000 = 900) instead of the smaller net interest income of 720, then added 20.

options.label: EUR 1,120m
options.why: Used gross interest income of 1,100 (no expense netting, no cap), then added 20.

takeaway: The cap only bites when net interest income exceeds 2.25% of assets. Here 720 is below 900, so it passes through unchanged.

reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
setup: Basel III standardized operational risk. Ten-year average annual operating loss is EUR 80m (high-quality data) and the business indicator component BIC is EUR 900m. Loss component LC = 15 × average loss. ILM = ln[e − 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8] and capital = BIC × ILM, with no supervisory override.
ask: Capital compared with the BIC of EUR 900m is:

options.label: Below EUR 900m
options.why: Forgot the 15× and compared the raw EUR 80m loss with BIC: that would give ILM about 0.62 and capital about EUR 559m.

options.label: Equal to EUR 900m
options.why: ILM equals 1 only when LC = BIC. Here LC is 1,200, above BIC.

takeaway: ILM is exactly 1 when LC equals BIC. A loss history that puts LC above BIC pushes capital above the BIC.

reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
setup: Basel III business indicator for a European bank, EUR bn, years 20X6 to 20X9. ILDC: 0.95, 1.3, 1.8, 1.6. Services SC: 1.6, 2.2, 2.6, 1.8. Financial FC (absolute): 0.5, 1.1, 1.3, 1.5. BI is the sum of the three components, each averaged over the latest three years (ending 20X9).
ask: The BI at 31 December 20X9 is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 1.7bn
options.why: Averaged the three components and then divided by 3 again.

options.label: ≈ EUR 15bn
options.why: Summed the three years without averaging.

options.label: ≈ EUR 51bn
options.why: Decimal slip: ten times the true figure.

takeaway: BI averages each component over the latest three years, so 20X6 drops out and the total is the sum of three averages.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I off-balance-sheet items, EUR m: transaction-related standby letters of credit 80, counterparty an OECD bank (CCF 50%); undrawn two-year commitment to corporates 200 (CCF 20%); undrawn six-month commitment to corporates 150 (CCF 0%). Risk weights: OECD bank 20%, corporate 100%.
ask: The off-balance-sheet RWA (EUR m) is closest to:

options.why: Counted only the standby letters of credit (40 × 20%) and dropped the two-year commitment.
Put the standby letters of credit at the corporate 100% weight instead of the OECD-bank 20%: 40 + 40.
Counted the six-month commitments at 100% of face value. A 0% CCF removes them entirely.

takeaway: Convert with the CCF first, then apply the counterparty's risk weight. Short commitments at 0% CCF add nothing.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: A G-SIB's private-sector credit exposures and the countercyclical buffer (CCyB) rate of each country: home country X 50% of exposures at 1.0%; country Y 30% at 2.5%; country Z 20% at 0.0%.

options.why: Used the home-country rate alone. The buffer follows where the exposures are, not where the bank is based.
Took the simple average of the three national rates instead of weighting by exposure.
Used the highest national rate.

takeaway: A bank's CCyB is the exposure-weighted average of the national buffers where its credit exposures sit.
